title: Aldosterone-secreting adrenal adenoma (zona glomerulosa): paresthesia and muscle weakness
vignette: A 45-year-old woman comes to the office due to a 4-month history of headaches and blurred vision. She takes no medications and has no other medical conditions. After the initial laboratory work-up, a CT scan of the abdomen is performed that reveals a 2-cm left-sided adrenal mass. The patient undergoes an uncomplicated left-sided adrenalectomy. Gross examination of the adrenal gland demonstrates a well-defined yellowish tumor within the cortex. Further evaluation reveals that the tumor cells are functionally similar to cells from the outermost hormone-producing layer of the adrenal cortex. This patient would most likely have had which of the following additional symptoms?

clues.note: Headaches and blurred vision suggest hypertension - consistent with an aldosterone-secreting tumor causing sodium retention and elevated blood pressure.

clues.text: well-defined yellowish tumor within the cortex
clues.note: A well-circumscribed yellow cortical tumor is an adrenocortical adenoma (lipid-rich cells). Its hormone output depends on which cortical layer it resembles.

clues.text: outermost hormone-producing layer of the adrenal cortex
clues.note: The OUTERMOST cortical layer is the zona glomerulosa, which produces ALDOSTERONE. So this is an aldosterone-secreting adenoma (primary hyperaldosteronism/Conn syndrome).

whatMatters: A cortical adenoma resembling the OUTERMOST layer (zona glomerulosa) secretes ALDOSTERONE = primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn syndrome). Excess aldosterone drives renal K+ and H+ loss -> HYPOKALEMIA (and metabolic alkalosis), causing PARESTHESIA and MUSCLE WEAKNESS (plus hypertension). Answer C.
strategy: Map cortical layer to hormone: 'GFR = Salt, Sugar, Sex' (glomerulosa->aldosterone, fasciculata->cortisol, reticularis->androgens). Outermost = aldosterone -> hypertension + hypokalemia -> weakness/paresthesia (answer C). Reject symptoms of other tumors: carcinoid (diarrhea/flushing), androgen excess (hirsutism), pheochromocytoma/medulla (sweating/tremor), Cushing/cortisol (weight gain, easy bruising).

eliminations.label: Diarrhea and flushing - carcinoid syndrome
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: episodic diarrhea and flushing from a serotonin-secreting neuroendocrine (carcinoid) tumor. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: that's a GI neuroendocrine tumor, not an aldosterone-producing adrenal adenoma. ✅ Correct if: carcinoid syndrome (serotonin).

eliminations.label: Excessive hair growth - androgen excess (zona reticularis)
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: hirsutism from excess androgens. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: androgens come from the INNERMOST layer (zona reticularis), not the outermost; this tumor makes aldosterone. ✅ Correct if: an androgen-secreting adrenal tumor.

eliminations.label: Sweating and tremulousness - pheochromocytoma (medulla)
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: catecholamine excess (sweating, tremor, palpitations) from a pheochromocytoma. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: those arise from the adrenal MEDULLA, not the cortex. ✅ Correct if: a catecholamine-secreting medullary tumor.

eliminations.label: Weight gain and easy bruising - Cushing (zona fasciculata)
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: cortisol excess (central weight gain, easy bruising, thin skin). ❌ WHY IT FAILS: cortisol is made by the MIDDLE layer (zona fasciculata), not the outermost. ✅ Correct if: a cortisol-secreting adrenal tumor (Cushing).

reasoning: A well-defined yellow cortical adenoma resembling the OUTERMOST layer (zona glomerulosa) secretes aldosterone
Primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn syndrome): aldosterone drives renal Na+ retention and K+/H+ excretion
Hypokalemia causes muscle weakness and paresthesia; answer C
mechanism: Adrenocortical adenomas secrete hormones according to the cortical layer they resemble: the OUTERMOST zona glomerulosa makes aldosterone, the middle zona fasciculata makes cortisol, and the inner zona reticularis makes androgens ('GFR - Salt, Sugar, Sex'). A tumor functionally similar to the outermost layer causes primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn syndrome). Aldosterone acts on the renal collecting ducts to reabsorb sodium and secrete potassium and hydrogen ions, producing hypertension with HYPOKALEMIA and metabolic alkalosis. Hypokalemia hyperpolarizes cells and impairs neuromuscular function, causing muscle cramps, MUSCLE WEAKNESS, and PARESTHESIA. (Extravascular volume overload/edema is usually minimal because of 'aldosterone escape.') The distractor symptoms belong to carcinoid (serotonin), androgen excess (zona reticularis), pheochromocytoma (adrenal medulla), and cortisol excess/Cushing (zona fasciculata).

difficulty.label: 📚 Pure knowledge gap
difficulty.message: First Aid Endo > adrenal cortex zones and hormones (GFR: aldosterone/cortisol/androgens); Conn syndrome -> hypertension + hypokalemia -> weakness/paresthesia; aldosterone escape.

difficulty.label: 🧭 Understanding the question
difficulty.message: Convert 'outermost layer' to zona glomerulosa/aldosterone, then predict the hypokalemia symptoms.

difficulty.label: 🔤 Vocabulary
difficulty.message: Unsure on zona glomerulosa/fasciculata/reticularis, aldosterone, hypokalemia, or paresthesia? Tell me which.

difficulty.label: 🧲 Pulled by a distractor
difficulty.message: Each distractor matches a DIFFERENT adrenal source: cortisol/Cushing (fasciculata), androgens (reticularis), catecholamines (medulla), serotonin (carcinoid).

difficulty.label: 🖼️ Imaging / diagram
difficulty.message: On the adrenal-cortex diagram, the outer band under the capsule is the zona glomerulosa (aldosterone). Anchor: 'outermost = salt = aldosterone.'

difficulty.label: ✍️ Something else
difficulty.message: Bank: outermost cortex = zona glomerulosa = aldosterone -> Conn syndrome (HTN + hypokalemia) -> weakness/paresthesia.

memoryHook: Outermost layer = salt layer = aldosterone. Too much salt hormone dumps potassium - weak, tingly, and hypertensive (Conn).
